title: salla sutta
credit: Pāḷi text and English translation as in Mor’s Pāḷi Workshop booklet.
groupSub: The Nearest Cause for the Origination of dukkha

paras.en:
“Bhikkhus, the uninstructed ordinary person feels
a pleasant vedanā, a painful vedanā,
and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant vedanā.

The instructed noble disciple too feels
a pleasant vedanā, a painful vedanā,
and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant vedanā.

Therein, bhikkhus, what is the distinction,
the disparity, the difference between the instructed noble disciple and the uninstructed ordinary person?”

“Venerable sir, our Dhamma is rooted in the
Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One,
and has the Blessed One as its refuge.
It would be good if the Blessed One would clear up the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from him, the bhikkhus will remember it.”

“Then listen and attend closely, bhikkhus,
I will speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the bhikkhus replied.
The Blessed One said this:

“Bhikkhus, when the uninstructed ordinary person
is being contacted by a painful vedanā,
he sorrows, grieves, and laments;
he weeps beating his breast and becomes bewildered.
He feels two vedanā — a bodily one and a mental one.

Suppose someone were to strike a man with a dart,
and then strike him immediately afterwards with a second dart, so that the man would feel a vedanā caused by two darts.

So too, when the uninstructed ordinary person is being contacted by a painful vedanā, he sorrows, grieves,
and laments… he feels two vedanā —
a bodily one and a mental one.

Being contacted by that same painful vedanā,
he harbors aversion towards it.
When he harbors aversion towards painful vedanā,
the latent tendency to aversion towards
painful vedanā lies behind this.

Being contacted by painful vedanā,
he seeks delight in sensual pleasure. For what reason?

Because the uninstructed ordinary person does not know of a way out of painful vedanā other than sensual pleasure. When he seeks delight in sensual pleasure,
the latent tendency to craving for pleasant vedanā
lies behind this.

He does not understand as it really is the origin and
the passing away, the gratification, the danger,
and the way out in the case of these vedanā.

When he does not understand these things,
the latent tendency to ignorance in regard to
neither-painful-nor-pleasant vedanā lies behind this.

If he feels a pleasant vedanā, he feels it attached.
If he feels a painful vedanā, he feels it attached.
If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant vedanā,
he feels it attached.

Bhikkhus, when the instructed noble disciple is contacted by a painful vedanā, he does not sorrow, grieve, or lament; he does not weep beating his breast and become bewildered.
He feels one vedanā — a bodily one, not a mental one.

Suppose someone were to strike a man with a dart,
but not strike him immediately afterwards with
a second dart, so that the man would feel
a vedanā caused by one dart only.

So too, when the instructed noble disciple is contacted by a painful vedanā he does not sorrow,
grieve, or lament; he does not weep beating his breast and become bewildered.

He feels one vedanā — a bodily one, not a mental one.
Being contacted by that same painful vedanā,
he harbors no aversion towards it.
Since he harbors no aversion towards painful vedanā, the latent tendency to aversion towards painful vedanā does not lie behind this.

Being contacted by painful vedanā, he does not seek delight in sensual pleasure. For what reason?
Because the instructed noble disciple knows of a way out from painful vedanā other than sensual pleasure.

Since he does not seek delight in sensual pleasure,
the latent tendency to craving for pleasant vedanā
does not lie behind this.
He understands as it really is the origin
and the passing away, the gratification, the danger,
and the way out in the case of these vedanā.
Since he understands these things, the latent tendency to ignorance in regard to neither-painful-nor-pleasant vedanā does not lie behind this.

If he feels a pleasant vedanā, he feels it unattached.
If he feels a painful vedanā, he feels it unattached.
If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant vedanā,
he feels it unattached.

This, bhikkhus, is called a noble disciple who is unattached to birth, aging, and death; who is unattached to sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection,
and misery; who is unattached to dukkha, I say.

This, bhikkhus, is the distinction, the disparity,
the difference between the instructed noble disciple
and the uninstructed ordinary person.”
